sentences.text: What if this is not a monster's scream at all, but the purest terror you have ever seen?
This is Medusa, painted by Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio in 1597.
And this isn't a cursed monster.
It's a boy with snakes for hair.
Pale, screaming, almost alive.
But look at his eyes.
He's screaming.
There's a white glint in each wide open eye.
And yet it doesn't feel like rage to you.
Look into his eyes.
There's terror there.
A sudden, helpless, conscious terror.
As if he knows you are the last thing he sees.
According to the traditional story of Medusa, anyone who looked at her was turned to stone.
And Caravaggio seems to capture something strange.
Not the monster's death, but the second right after it.
The moment when the head still understands what has happened.
Imagine giving a monster your own face.
Would you paint yourself as the hero?
Would you leave yourself out of it?
Or would you become the monster yourself?
That's what makes this painting so hard to look at.
The face is still young, but his eyes no longer look innocent.
His open mouth says one thing, his frown says another.
And perhaps that's the most frightening part.
Maybe terror does not begin with monsters.
Maybe it begins with a mirror, then becomes a mask, and eventually turns into terror.
So look at him one more time.
Do you see a monster in its final second?
Or a painter screaming at his own face?

meta.title: Caravaggio painted his own face on Medusa
meta.description: Caravaggio painted Medusa on a round wooden shield around 1597; it hangs in the Uffizi in Florence. He gave the severed Gorgon's head his own face.
meta.question: A monster in its final second, or a painter screaming at himself?

sources.claim: Although the work is not signed or dated, it is often dated as 1597.
Medusa was once a human woman, but the goddess Athena cursed her to live as a monster after Poseidon raped her in one of Athena's temples.
Her hair was turned to snakes, and anybody who looked at her would be turned to stone.
Though the head is decapitated, it still appears conscious, with the painting capturing its final moments before death.
The face's eyes are widened, and its brows are creased; its mouth hangs open.
